original_value: Intermittently-powered embedded devices (IPDs) are getting wide-spread attention these days. However, running periodic real-time tasks on these devices remains a challenging problem due to the lack of support for data freshness guarantees, timekeeping, and schedulability analysis. Especially, while many sensing tasks require long atomic operations for data acquisition from sensors, most prior work on IPDs assumes compute-only workloads and disregards such sensor operations. In this paper, we present a new energy scheduling scheme to execute periodic real-time tasks with atomic sensing operations. Our scheme keeps track of time and ensures the periodic execution of sensing tasks while efficiently utilizing intermittent power sources. We provide schedulability analysis to determine if a task is schedulable in a given charging setup, and extend this idea for scheduling multiple tasks. As a proof-of-concept, we design a custom programmable RFID tag device, called R'tag, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed techniques in a realistic sensing application. We compare the baseline approach and the proposed scheme in both simulation and real platforms. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms the baseline approach in terms of task scheduling, timekeeping, and periodic sensing.

result.paraphrase: Intermittently powered embedded devices (IPDs) have recently drawn widespread attention. Yet executing periodic real-time tasks on them remains difficult because support is lacking for data freshness guarantees, timekeeping, and schedulability analysis. This is especially true since many sensing tasks need long atomic sensor-data acquisition operations, while most earlier IPD research assumes compute-only workloads and ignores sensor operations. In this paper, we introduce a new energy scheduling scheme for periodic real-time tasks that include atomic sensing operations. Our scheme tracks time, guarantees periodic execution of sensing tasks, and uses intermittent power sources efficiently. We also present schedulability analysis to decide whether a task can be scheduled under a given charging setup, and extend the approach to multiple-task scheduling. As a proof of concept, we build a custom programmable RFID tag device called R'tag and demonstrate the proposed techniques in a realistic sensing application. We evaluate both the baseline and proposed schemes on simulation and real hardware. Experimental results show that our method outperforms the baseline in task scheduling, timekeeping, and periodic sensing.
